vignette: John, a 54-year-old European man in a relationship and working as a civil servant, experienced significant trauma when he was physically abused by his romantic partner. The abuse left deep emotional scars that have manifested in various symptoms over time. The traumatic event itself began with an argument that escalated into a violent confrontation. John vividly remembers the taste of metal from a ring worn by his abuser during the assault and the feeling of helplessness as he lost control of the situation. These memories have become powerful triggers for him, especially when he finds himself in situations where he lacks control or is alone with men. Since the event, John has developed several maladaptive strategies to cope with the distressing memories. He avoids sleeping alone or being in unfamiliar places, often insisting on staying at his partner’s home or other familiar locations. Being alone in a room or building fills him with dread, and he feels safest when constantly surrounded by people. This constant socializing is not just a preference but a necessity for John to avoid the overwhelming thoughts of losing control. The vividness of these memories has made it difficult for John to recall specific details deliberately. When the memories do return, they are like snapshots from a photo album in his mind, often accompanied by the metallic taste he experienced during the assault. This photographic recall and sensory vividness contribute significantly to his sense of loss of control when triggered. John’s triggers have reinforced his maladaptive strategies. The fear of losing control and being alone with men drives him to maintain a constant social presence, avoiding any situation where he might be alone or in an unfamiliar setting. For instance, at work, he frequently stays late, making sure someone else is always around before leaving the office, even though this has led to strained relationships with his colleagues who find his behavior somewhat odd. The memory detachment John employs as a coping mechanism has made it hard for him to fully process what happened during the traumatic event. When he tries to deliberately recall the incident, he finds himself unable to access the details clearly, which only serves to heighten his anxiety and reinforce the fear of losing control again. His avoidance behaviors have become a self-reinforcing cycle: he avoids situations that trigger memories, but these very strategies prevent him from addressing the underlying trauma. Recently, John has begun to recognize that his coping mechanisms are no longer sustainable. The constant need for socialization and avoiding solitude has taken a toll on his relationships and work life. His partner expresses concern over his extreme avoidance behaviors, and colleagues at the office have started to view him as overly dependent and difficult to manage. These changes in his daily environment have become a source of significant distress. John’s most pressing fear is that he will lose control again, just like during the traumatic event. He is desperately hoping for relief from these overwhelming feelings and is now seeking help to find more adaptive ways to cope with his trauma. His current state reflects an acute need to regain some semblance of normalcy in his life while confronting the lingering effects of the abuse.
